interest: This file provides valuable historical insight into economic conditions, nutritional standards, and occupation governance in Japan in the spring of 1949. First, it documents the transition away from emergency occupation relief policies: SCAP and the Japanese Government phased out special supplementary food rations for foreign nationals as Japan's domestic food supply stabilized (reaching 1,500–1,600 calories per day) and free markets re-emerged. Second, it captures the logistical challenges faced by private American organizations like the YMCA attempting to calculate living expenses and benchmark inflation against 1937 pre-war standards. Third, the file illustrates the institutional division of responsibility between the Department of State in Washington and SCAP in Tokyo, showing that the State Department lacked detailed Japanese cost-of-living data because its personnel were integrated into the occupation structure. Finally, it records the 270 yen-to-the-dollar exchange rate for American civilians in early April 1949, mere weeks before the implementation of the Dodge Line established the unified 360 yen rate.

overview: This file (decimal file 894.5017) contains State Department correspondence from March and April 1949 concerning economic statistics, living costs, currency exchange rates, and food rationing in occupied Japan. It comprises two main exchanges: first, Despatch No. 189 from U.S. Political Adviser William J. Sebald in Tokyo (accompanied by a State Department Central Records replacement copy sheet and SCAP Diplomatic Section Note to the Australian Mission) notifying the Secretary of State that the Japanese Government would cease providing supplementary food rations to foreign residents on May 1, 1949, as basic ration levels had improved to 1,500–1,600 calories per day; and second, an inquiry from the International Committee of the YMCA regarding 1937 versus 1949 Japanese living costs and dollar exchange rates for American civilians, along with the State Department's reply referring the YMCA to SCAP's Economic and Scientific Section and citing the official exchange rate of 270 yen to the dollar.

subfiles.about: Transmits SCAPIN 1947 and a diplomatic note concerning the termination of supplementary food rations provided by the Japanese Government to foreign nationals residing in Japan.
subfiles.summary: United States Political Adviser William J. Sebald forwards documentation regarding the discontinuation of special food rations for foreign residents in Japan. The despatch encloses copies of SCAPIN 1947 and a Diplomatic Section note of March 26, 1949, which relieve the Japanese Government of the obligation to provide supplementary rations after May 1, 1949. Page 1 contains a Department of State Division of Communications and Records (DC/R) replacement form designating this copy as the official record copy for decimal file 894.5017/3-3049 in lieu of the missing original action copy.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 189 on Supplementary Food Rations for Foreign Nationals in Japan (with Record Copy Replacement Form)

subfiles.about: Informs the Australian Mission that the Japanese Government will no longer provide supplementary food rations to foreign nationals residing in Japan after May 1, 1949.
subfiles.from: Diplomatic Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.summary: The Diplomatic Section of GHQ/SCAP notifies the Australian Mission in Japan that foreign nationals will no longer receive Japanese Government supplementary rations after May 1, 1949. The note explains that these rations had been instituted in 1946 when the Japanese basic ration was nutritionally inadequate and black/free markets were unavailable. Because the standard Japanese ration now provides 1,500 to 1,600 calories per day and commercial supplementary foodstuffs are accessible, special foreign rations are no longer necessary.
subfiles.title: Diplomatic Section Note to Australian Mission on Supplementary Food Rations for Foreign Nationals in Japan (Enclosure No. 2 to Despatch No. 189)

subfiles.about: Answers a YMCA inquiry regarding living costs in Japan and states the official currency exchange rate of 270 yen to the dollar.
subfiles.summary: Max W. Bishop, Chief of the Division of Northeast Asian Affairs, replies to the International Committee of the YMCA's letter of April 1, 1949. He explains that the Department of State does not maintain figures on the current cost of living in Japan because its personnel are integrated into the occupation establishment. He advises the YMCA to contact SCAP's Economic and Scientific Section in Tokyo for cost-of-living data and states that the current official exchange rate is 270 yen to the dollar.
subfiles.title: Letter from Department of State (Bishop) to International Committee of YMCA on Cost of Living and Exchange Rate
subfiles.to: International Committee of Young Men's Christian Associations

subfiles.about: Requests data on the current cost of living in Japan compared to 1937 and asks for the dollar exchange rate available to American civilians.
subfiles.summary: Lee M. Terrill of the International Committee of Young Men's Christian Associations writes to the Department of State's Far Eastern Division (Japan Desk). The organization seeks comparative figures or estimation methodologies for the cost of living in Japan in 1949 relative to 1937. Terrill also asks for the current exchange rate for U.S. dollars available to American civilians residing in Japan.
subfiles.title: Letter from International Committee of YMCA (Terrill) to Department of State Requesting Cost of Living and Exchange Rate Information
subfiles.to: Department of State (Far Eastern Division, Japan Desk)
